entities.summary:
Ludovico Prodocator (d. September 4, 1504) was a prominent Greek Cypriot cardinal whose career at the apex of the Catholic Church during the late 15th and early 16th centuries underscored the Church's international reach and the diverse origins of its leadership. As Bishop of Capaccio from 1485 and subsequently elevated to cardinal by Pope Alexander VI in 1500, Prodocator navigated the complex political and religious landscape of the Italian Renaissance, bridging Hellenic heritage with the Latin ecclesiastical hierarchy. His tenure coincided with a period of intense papal consolidation of power and significant diplomatic maneuvering, positioning him as a figure privy to the era's major ecclesiastical and political developments.

Prodocator’s ecclesiastical ascent began with his appointment as Bishop of Capaccio, a diocese in the Kingdom of Naples, in 1485, a role he maintained until his death. His elevation to the cardinalate by Pope Alexander VI on September 28, 1500, within the consistory that also created other notable figures, marked the zenith of his career. As Cardinal-Deacon of Sant'Agata dei Goti, he became an active member of the papal curia, likely participating in various congregations and diplomatic efforts crucial to the Borgia papacy, which sought to reassert its temporal and spiritual authority across Italy and Europe.

His career exemplifies the cosmopolitan nature of the late medieval Church, where individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds could achieve high office in Rome. Prodocator's presence in the College of Cardinals during the turbulent Borgia years contributed to the diplomatic and administrative functions of the Holy See, influencing decisions on ecclesiastical appointments, papal finance, and international relations. His death in Rome in 1504 occurred just a year after the passing of his patron, Pope Alexander VI, marking the end of a significant era in papal history.
